foreign_origin_routes.published_etymology: Traditionally derived from πορφύρω (porphúrō, “I redden”), itself related to φύρω (phúrō, “I mix”), Hittite 𒁍𒊒𒌓 (purut, “mud, soil”), Sanskrit भुरति (bhuráti, “have convulsions, sprawl”). dictionary_entry.etymology_text: Traditionally derived from πορφύρω (porphúrō, “I redden”), itself related to φύρω (phúrō, “I mix”), Hittite 𒁍𒊒𒌓 (purut, “mud, soil”), Sanskrit भुरति (bhuráti, “have convulsions, sprawl”). However, Beekes does not dismiss a Pre-Greek origin, in view of the absence of connections in other Indo-European languages.

Uncertain. Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀡𐀮𐀅𐀃𐀚 (po-se-da-o-ne); possibly from a vocative *Πότ(ε)ι Δᾶς (*Pót(e)i Dâs) from πόσις (pósis, “master, husband”) and *Δα (*Da) (Γῆ (Gê), see Δημήτηρ (Dēmḗtēr) and Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀚𐀯𐀅𐀃𐀚 (e-ne-si-da-o-ne), which would be cognate with ἐννοσίγαιος (ennosígaios)).

Uncertain, though most theories imply a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *peth₂- (“to spread out; to fly”) by relating the term to reflexes as such: * πῑ́πτω (pī́ptō, “to fall”), thus a "waterfall" > "river that sweeps things away", * πετᾰ́ννῡμῐ (petắnnūmĭ, “to spread out”) and Proto-Germanic *faþmaz (“embrace”), thus an "extension of water", * πέτομαι (pétomai, “to fly”), particularly the third-person singular aorist middle indicative form ἔπτᾰτο (éptăto) which is close in form, thus a "flying stream of water". Other theories relate the term to πόντος (póntos, “sea”) < Proto-Indo-European *pónteh₁s (“path, bridge”), or to Proto-Indo-European *kweth₂- (“to bubble, foam”).
Indefinite form of interrogative πότε (póte, “when?”).
